case_analysis.thread_summary: This thread (August–September 2025) covers the Bluetooth SIG certification planning for an automotive in-vehicle connectivity unit (Volvo UXC, developed by Alps Alpine [COMPANY] with a Qualcomm SoC directly mounted on PCB). The thread involves multiple parties: Alps Alpine (customer, infotainment system developer), Volvo (vehicle OEM), Qualcomm (SoC/chipset vendor), and Ariion (certification service). Key topics: (1) Power Class 2 vs. Class 1 inconsistency with the included Qualcomm Host DN (Q366226), requiring a Subset request to Qualcomm; (2) RF PHY test scope for automotive - what modes are needed (Coded not needed, 2M likely needed, scope determined by product app not included DN); (3) IOPT test exemption under QPRDv4 when Host DN covers product profiles at ICS level; (4) Core-Controller DN creation as a future-proofing strategy against chip vendor DN updates. The quote evolved from a provisional ¥2,600,000 (before Qualcomm DN was confirmed) to a final ¥2,000,000 (RF full ¥1,200,000 + RF PHY 1M only ¥400,000 + proxy ¥250,000 + CF ¥150,000), with a new Component DN from Qualcomm also resolving the Power Class ICS issue.
all_questions_found: Our product targets Power Class 2 but the included Qualcomm DN has LL ICS 9/11 (Power Class 1) = YES. Does this cause a Power Class inconsistency, and how do we fix it without triggering a massive LL test plan?
Is the RF PHY test scope determined by the included chip vendor DN, or by our product's application? For an automotive in-vehicle unit, do we need Coded PHY and 2M PHY?
Are IOPT interoperability tests required, or are they exempt because the product's profiles are ICS-level covered by the Qualcomm Host DN?
If we register Core-Complete only and Qualcomm later updates their Host DN, will we need to redo RF testing? Would creating a Core-Controller DN now protect against future RF re-testing?
case_analysis.key_technical_discussion: Three advanced registration strategy principles are demonstrated: (1) Power Class ICS inconsistency resolution: changing LL 9/11 to NO directly triggers the full LL Test Plan under the post-July 2024 system; the solution is to request the chip vendor create a Subset with those ICS items pre-set to NO. When the Qualcomm DN also unusually includes RF PHY layers, the Subset request must cover LL 9/11, RF 1/15, and RF 1/1. A new Qualcomm Component DN issued mid-thread already had LL 9/11:NO and no RF/RF PHY layers, resolving the issue without a Subset. (2) RF PHY scope is product-application-determined, not DN-determined. For automotive: Coded not needed; 2M needed if peer device (phone) could auto-negotiate; custom BLE profile (128-bit UUID) makes 1M+2M mandatory. (3) Core-Controller DN as insurance: creates a product-owned RF evidence anchor that survives chip vendor DN updates; costs 2x SIG Qualification Fee but same service fee.
case_analysis.key_decision_logic: Subset requests to chip vendors are the correct solution when including a DN with Power Class ICS conflicts (not direct ICS changes, which trigger test plans). RF PHY test scope must be confirmed with the product application team, not inferred from the included DN. IOPT exemption applies when the Host DN's ICS covers the product's profiles - this is a content-based exemption, not a deadline-based one. Core-Controller DN creation is a strategic long-term cost management decision for products in ecosystems with frequent chip vendor DN updates (e.g., annual Android platform updates).
case_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: Direct LL ICS changes instead of Subset requests trigger hundreds of unexpected test items. Inferring RF PHY test scope from the included DN (rather than product application) leads to incorrect test scope - either overtesting or undertesting. Missing the IOPT exemption when it applies causes unnecessary overquoting. Not recommending Core-Controller DN for automotive products with long lifecycles may result in repeated RF re-testing costs.
case_analysis.consulting_takeaway: For Qualcomm-based automotive products: (1) Always check all Power Class ICS items across all layers (LL, RF, RF PHY) in the included DN before planning registration - request a Subset if changes are needed, not direct ICS edits; (2) Ask the customer's product application team to confirm RF PHY feature support - do not infer from the DN; (3) Check for IOPT exemption via Host DN ICS coverage before quoting IOPT tests; (4) Proactively discuss Core-Controller DN strategy with customers in ecosystems where the chip vendor's Host DN updates annually, as it is a multi-year cost-saving decision.
